plain_english:
But suppose your life has become a mess. You've stumbled into some trap — maybe set by politics or personal bad luck — and you can't escape. You can't untangle it or break free. Remember how prisoners suffer terribly at first from their chains. The weight hurts. The metal cuts. But once they stop fighting and accept their situation, something changes. Necessity teaches them to bear it with courage. Habit makes it feel lighter.

You can find moments of joy and peace in any situation — if you choose to take troubles lightly instead of hating them. We were born knowing we'd face sorrow. Nothing shows nature's kindness more than this: she gave us the ability to get used to things. Habit softens even the worst disasters. If misfortune kept hitting us with the same brutal force as that first blow, no one could survive it.
original_excerpt: Suppose, however, that your life has become full of trouble, and that without knowing what you were doing you have fallen into some snare which either public or private Fortune has set for you, and that you can neither untie it nor break it: then remember that fettered men suffer much at first from the burdens and clogs upon their legs: afterwards, when they have made up their minds not to fret themselves about them, but to endure them, necessity teaches them to bear them bravely, and habit to bear them easily. In every station of life you will find amusements, relaxations, and enjoyments; that is, provided you be willing to make light of evils rather than to hate them. Knowing to what sorrows we were born, there is nothing for which Nature more deserves our thanks than for having invented habit as an alleviation of misfortune, which soon accustoms us to the severest evils. No one could hold out against misfortune if it permanently exercised the same force as at its first onset.

plain_english: We are all chained to Fortune. Some people wear loose chains made of gold. Others wear tight chains made of cheaper metal. But what's the difference? We're all prisoners together. Even the people who bound us are bound themselves. Do you think a chain on your left hand is easier to carry? One person may be chained by public office, another by wealth. Some must bear the weight of noble birth, others of humble origins. Some obey other people's commands, some only their own. Some are stuck in one place by exile, others by being chosen as priests. All life is slavery. So each person should accept their situation. Complain as little as possible. Grab whatever good you can reach. No condition is so miserable that a fair mind can't find some compensation in it.
original_excerpt: We are all chained to Fortune: some men’s chain is loose and made of gold, that of others is tight and of meaner metal: but what difference does this make? we are all included in the same captivity, and even those who have bound us are bound themselves, unless you think that a chain on the left side is lighter to bear: one man may be bound by public office, another by wealth: some have to bear the weight of illustrious, some of humble birth: some are subject to the commands of others, some only to their own: some are kept in one place by being banished thither, others by being elected to the priesthood. All life is slavery: let each man therefore reconcile himself to his lot, complain of it as little as possible, and lay hold of whatever good lies within his reach. No condition can be so wretched that an impartial mind can find no compensations in it. Small sites, if ingeniously divided, may be made use of for many different purposes, and arrangement will render ever so narrow a room habitable.

plain_english: Small spaces can serve many purposes if you divide them cleverly. Good planning can make even the narrowest room livable. Use common sense to handle problems. You can soften what's harsh, expand what's cramped, and make heavy burdens lighter if you carry them skillfully. Don't let your desires roam too far. Keep them focused on what's nearby, since they won't tolerate being completely shut down. Leave alone things that can't happen or are very difficult to achieve. Go after things that are close and within reach of your hopes. Always remember that all things are equally unimportant. They may look different on the outside, but inside they're all equally empty.
original_excerpt: Call good sense to your aid against difficulties: it is possible to soften what is harsh, to widen what is too narrow, and to make heavy burdens press less severely upon one who bears them skilfully. Moreover, we ought not to allow our desires to wander far afield, but we must make them confine themselves to our immediate neighbourhood, since they will not endure to be altogether locked up. We must leave alone things which either cannot come to pass or can only be effected with difficulty, and follow after such things as are near at hand and within reach of our hopes, always remembering that all things are equally unimportant, and that though they have a different outward appearance, they are all alike empty within. Neither let us envy those who are in high places: the heights which look lofty to us are steep and rugged. Again, those whom unkind fate has placed in critical situations will be safer if they show as little pride in their proud position as may be, and do all they are able to bring down their fortunes to the level of other men’s.

plain_english: Don't envy people in high positions. Those heights that look impressive to us are steep and dangerous. And those whom cruel fate has put in risky situations will be safer if they show less pride in their position. They should do everything they can to bring their fortunes down to everyone else's level. Many people have to cling to their high places of power because they can't come down except by falling hard. Yet they tell us their biggest burden is being forced to burden others. They say they're nailed to their high post rather than lifted up to it. So let them hand out justice, mercy, and kindness freely and generously. This will give them help to cushion their fall. Looking ahead to this will help them hold their position with more hope. But nothing frees us from these swings between hope and fear like setting some limit on our success. Don't let Fortune choose when to stop your career. Stop on your own, long before you apparently need to. If you do this, certain desires will still stir your spirit. But since they're kept within bounds, they won't lead you into huge and uncertain ventures.
original_excerpt: There are many who must needs cling to their high pinnacle of power, because they cannot descend from it save by falling headlong: yet they assure us that their greatest burden is being obliged to be burdensome to others, and that they are nailed to their lofty post rather than raised to it: let them then, by dispensing justice, clemency, and kindness with an open and liberal hand, provide themselves with assistance to break their fall, and looking forward to this maintain their position more hopefully. Yet nothing sets us free from these alternations of hope and fear so well as always fixing some limit to our successes, and not allowing Fortune to choose when to stop our career, but to halt of our own accord long before we apparently need do so. By acting thus certain desires will rouse up our spirits, and yet being confined within bounds, will not lead us to embark on vast and vague enterprises.
